title: Understand the system you own
summary: A practical course in how StreamCore works, why its boundaries exist, and where to make your next change.
body:
You already know Android and TV development. The difficult part here is reconstructing decisions made by someone else: why a request crosses several types, where rules execute, which state is authoritative, and what a small change might affect. This guide makes those decisions visible.

The target architecture is backend-agnostic. StreamCore applications and external applications use the same public SDK. A provider connects that SDK to a particular backend. Android screens, TV focus, navigation and player rendering remain application responsibilities.

Learn in order

Start with modules and contracts. Follow one SDK instance through login and profile entry. Then study catalogue, playback and persistence before changing code.

Start with the module map →

Investigate a specific operation

Use a request walkthrough, then open the actual implementation beside each explanation. The source explorer includes the SDK source snapshot and relevant application consumers.

Follow a request →

The problem this SDK solves

Imagine Android, web and a future client each implementing search history, resume thresholds and account isolation independently. Small decisions would diverge: one records every keystroke, another records submissions; one resumes nearly completed films, another starts again. The SDK places those common rules behind operations that every consumer uses.

Providers still differ. TMDB has a particular login protocol and catalogue schema. ClientB simulates a second backend. The runtime should not learn TMDB URLs or DTO names. Instead, the provider implements narrow contracts that speak StreamCore models.

Three kinds of code to recognize

KindQuestion it answersExample
Public contractWhat can an SDK consumer ask for, and what does it receive?SearchService.search, StreamCoreContent
Shared behaviorWhat must consistently happen around this operation?Normalize a query, require the authorized profile, apply history rules.
Backend implementationHow does this backend perform the request?Call TMDB search, map its DTOs, classify its errors.

The same distinction exists for storage: the runtime decides whose progress to update and whether it is resumable; the store persists the entry. A service that only delegates is worth questioning. A boundary that contains provider-specific protocol or preserves one shared owner has a stronger reason to exist.

How to read an operation

  1. Start at the public method. Read its parameters, return type, KDoc and capabilities.
  2. Find the runtime implementation. Identify validation, context capture, provider/store calls and result handling.
  3. Follow the shared guard once. Understand its before/after checks. On later readings you can recognize its contract without re-reading every line.
  4. Follow the provider or store. This is where transport or persistence actually happens.
  5. Read a behavioral test. Use it to confirm a specific rule, not as a replacement for understanding the implementation.

For a first exercise, read these two small files in order: and . Notice that the client assembles services; it does not itself implement every feature.

What this guide gives you

  • Source-backed lessons with exact files and searchable code, available without an IDE.
  • Request walkthroughs showing where control goes, what state is read and what side effects happen.
  • Small educational simulations for profile activation, playback cadence and search history. These model selected rules; they do not execute Kotlin or contact a backend.
  • Reading exercises, knowledge checks and change recipes that connect understanding to maintenance.
Reading progress is your own checklist. Marking a lesson read does not measure understanding. Try explaining its operation in your own words, then use the exercise to find the relevant code. You do not need to memorize every DTO property.

Facts, reasons and possible changes

A statement such as “each valid invocation of the profile authorization guard fetches profiles” describes current behavior. “This centralizes checks” explains a benefit. “We might reduce those requests” is a possible design change with performance and authorization consequences. This guide keeps those categories separate. Understanding a choice does not require agreeing with it.

Your preference is now a project rule: do not add interfaces, files or callbacks merely for partial reuse or isolated tests. Keep related work easy to follow. Preserve meaningful backend, platform and persistence boundaries, and make tests fit the production design.

Scope and freshness

The course covers all SDK modules and the application boundaries needed to understand them. It is not a full course in Compose, Ktor, DataStore or coroutines, and it does not explain every screen layout. The source explorer is a snapshot of the working tree, including its uncommitted SDK changes, taken when this HTML was built. Build outputs and local credentials are excluded.

Android and Kotlin/Wasm are the current SDK targets. iOS/Swift and a JavaScript/TypeScript package are later work. The optional demo playback is sample media, not streaming rights or playable media for every catalogue title. These distinctions matter when deciding what the SDK is ready to promise.

quiz.question: Where should a shared rule such as when to save playback progress be enforced?
options: Behind the SDK's playback operations, with the application reporting playback events
quiz.explanation: Consumers report events and own rendering. Shared SDK operations enforce the same rule across consumers, while providers implement backend-specific work.

title: A map of the modules
summary: Learn which module owns each kind of code, and why a runtime call can travel against the compile-dependency direction.
body:
There are nine registered SDK projects: eight published modules and one non-published testing support project. They are not nine consecutive steps in every request. Some define types, some implement behavior, some connect a backend, and three provide optional presentation resources.

The testing project shares sources without publishing

:sdk:testing applies only Gradle's base plugin. It has no Kotlin/Android plugin, compilation, standalone test execution or publication. Its sdk/testing/src/commonTest/kotlin directory contains ProviderContract and its result assertion helper. Both providers include this directory in their own commonTest sources, keeping one copy of the common journeys. Their actual @Test functions still live beside each provider. Nothing in this folder is published as an SDK artifact or included in production source sets.

Sync Gradle after changing source roots. Then use a usage-search scope that excludes tests when following production callers; an all-usages search can still show test code.

A dependency is not a request

The main compile-dependency direction is provider → runtime → api → model. This means the provider module can refer to runtime contracts. It does not mean a request must begin in the provider implementation.

At execution time the application calls a public service, the runtime applies shared rules, and the runtime calls the provider object supplied during construction. The runtime only knows an interface such as AuthProvider. TMDB supplies an object that implements that interface. There is no runtime-to-TMDB Gradle dependency.

Compile dependencies: provider → runtime → api → model

Runtime calls:        application → runtime service → provider adapter
                                               ↘ local store

This is the concrete use of dependency inversion here. You do not need a framework to achieve it; constructor arguments wire the objects together.

Folder, package and artifact mean different things

ExampleMeaning
sdk/providers/tmdbDirectory on disk.
:sdk:providers:tmdbGradle project path used by build tasks and project dependencies.
com.pampoukidis.streamcore.sdk.providers.tmdbKotlin namespace used by imports.
com.pampoukidis.streamcore:provider-tmdb:0.1.0-alpha02Published coordinate consumed by another project.

Do not rename one and assume the others follow automatically. The publication convention deliberately maps module paths to artifacts. Kotlin package names and public declarations are compatibility surfaces of their own.

Inside a module directory

  • build.gradle.kts declares targets, dependencies and conventions. It is maintained source.
  • src/commonMain/kotlin contains portable Kotlin compiled for the enabled targets.
  • src/androidMain/kotlin contains Android-specific factories and persistence integration.
  • src/wasmJsMain/kotlin contains browser-specific code. Having commonMain alone does not establish browser support.
  • commonTest contains shared tests; host and browser source sets add platform-specific tests.
  • composeResources contains shared strings and artwork in optional presentation modules.
  • build/ contains generated output. Edit the source that generates it.
The old API snapshot directories are currently retired. :sdk:api is the consumer module. Gradle api(...) exports a dependency. The former api/*.api and api-android/*.api files were compatibility snapshots. These are three different uses of “API.” Snapshot checks remain deferred.

Why model types share a prefix

Every top-level type in :sdk:model uses StreamCore without a trailing Model. This makes ownership recognizable in a consumer that already has types named Profile or Error. Nested members stay short, such as StreamCoreResult.Success.

A provider DTO represents its wire format. A StreamCore model represents the SDK's meaning. A presentation state represents what the screen needs now. Those shapes need not match. Mapping is meaningful when it removes backend assumptions, not when it just copies an identical object to create another layer.

Provider response DTO → StreamCoreContent → screen rendering
                              ↓
                     saved content snapshot

Content collections preserve identity, purpose, items and ordering. The application decides poster layout, focus behavior and hero text formatting. Playback media describes a source; player engines render it outside the headless SDK.

The public keyword is not the whole audience

AuthProvider is public because another Gradle module must implement it. It is a provider integration contract, not the API a feature ViewModel should use. Conversely, AuthService is intended for consuming applications. Runtime service implementations are internal.

The source boundary gate prevents application features from importing runtime integration or storage code. It also checks provider/model naming and production dependency direction. Public visibility enables cross-module wiring; documentation and dependency scopes define the intended audience.

Read the structure from source

Try it: pick StreamCoreContent in the source explorer. Find its module, then find the provider mapper that produces it. Next find a ViewModel that consumes it. Explain why that ViewModel never needs the backend DTO.

quiz.question: How can RuntimeAuthService call TMDB without depending on the TMDB module?
options: The runtime imports TMDB dynamically by its package name
The provider factory supplies an object implementing the runtime-owned AuthProvider interface
The sdk-api module contains a copy of the TMDB implementation
quiz.explanation: The runtime depends on its own integration contract. The provider module depends on that contract and supplies its implementation during construction.

title: Keep the vocabulary straight
summary: A glossary of the concepts that make the implementation harder to read, with a practical way to check your understanding.
body:
Names you will repeatedly encounter

Client, service, provider, repository, store

Client: the SDK instance exposing configuration, capabilities, context and services. Service: an application-facing group of operations. Provider: a backend integration contract where backend work exists. Repository: the name used by many concrete provider/storage implementations. Store: a narrow local saved-data contract. These do not mandate five classes per operation.

Account, profile, selected profile, authorized profile

An account is the authenticated parent identity. A profile is a subprofile belonging to it. Selecting a profile is part of entry; a protected profile may still need PIN confirmation. An authorized profile is the current permission to run that profile's operations. A persisted selected-profile ID is not a restored permission grant.

Session, activation, captured authorization, stale result

AccountSession is an in-memory account identity plus account-bound adapters. AuthorizedProfile identifies one successful profile entry. Capturing authorization means retaining that particular object when an operation/observer/recorder starts. A result is stale when the current account or activation no longer matches it. Same profile ID does not imply same activation.

Restore session, logout, invalidate, close

sdk.auth.restoreSession() explicitly restores and validates persisted authentication. It returns current context once authentication is initialized; direct login does not require restoration first. Neither construction nor a remembered profile selection grants profile access. Logout requests backend sign-out and clears successful session context while retaining saved user data. Invalidation responds to authoritative rejection of an already invalid session. Close releases one SDK instance's owned resources and cancels its work. A closed instance is not reusable; closing is not remote logout.

Flow, StateFlow, context projection

A StateFlow represents a current value plus observations of changes. sdk.context projects internal account/profile/lifecycle state into a public immutable model. Stored-data methods return flows bound to their captured activation. The host owns its collector coroutine; closing the SDK does not promise that every host collector completes.

Mutex, atomic state, cancellation

A mutex serializes a related sequence of suspending actions. The runtime uses an authentication mutex for login/logout coordination and separate recorder mutexes for playback events. Atomic state updates change one immutable state snapshot without partially updating its fields. Coroutine cancellation stops work; it is rethrown rather than presented as an ordinary failure. Cancellation does not prove a remote or persisted side effect was rolled back.

Capability, authorization, policy, error

A capability says whether an operation is supported. Authorization says whether the current account/profile can perform it. Content policy interprets backend classifications. An error says why this particular attempt failed. Unsupported, Unauthorized and SessionExpired are different outcomes with different effects.

Snapshot, DTO, serialization

A DTO matches backend input/output. A content snapshot preserves SDK content fields alongside a saved entry, so local collections can render it. Serialization is the exact persisted representation, including field names/defaults. The current SDK reads and writes its namespaced format without importing old development data. Changes to serialized fields still need deliberate defaults and current-store restart checks.

Headless, platform target, optional UI

Headless means no screens, Compose UI, Koin or player rendering in the SDK's core dependency closure. It can still include platform-specific storage and HTTP engines. Android and Kotlin/Wasm are delivered targets. Optional SDK UI artifacts provide shared resource/presentation contracts; applications still render and navigate.

Public API, provider integration surface, API dependency scope

The consumer API is the service/model contract. Provider integration contracts are public across Gradle modules so providers can implement them. Gradle api exports a dependency to consumers' compilation; implementation keeps its types off that public compile surface while allowing runtime transitive resolution.

A maintenance reading checklist

Before changing an operation, be able to answer these questions using the code:

  1. Who calls it: application, runtime, provider, or store?
  2. What account/profile context does it capture, and when?
  3. Which validation and capability checks run before side effects?
  4. Where is the network request or storage write?
  5. What happens if cancellation arrives after a side effect?
  6. Which failures change session state and which preserve it?
  7. Does this change affect a public contract or a persisted representation?
  8. Which existing test demonstrates the expected behavior?

Exercises that demonstrate understanding

Explain a normal path: trace a successful submitted search. Point to normalization, backend request, policy filtering, history write and final context check. Then explain which of those runs for Typing.
Explain a state change: capture a progress recorder, leave and re-enter the same profile, then report a checkpoint using the old recorder. Predict the result before opening its implementation.
Explain a boundary: imagine adding a third provider. Identify the shared code it reuses, the contracts it implements, and the things a screen must never import.
Propose one simplification: choose a helper you find confusing. State its current side effects and invariants, then show a simpler call path preserving them. Judge it by readability and behavior, not a target class count.

How to keep this guide useful

Lessons are maintained under docs/tracked/sdk/guide-content; generated HTML lives under build/sdk-docs. After code changes, review the affected explanation and interactive rules, then run python tools/sdk/build-guide.py. The generator embeds a new source snapshot and fails on missing or ambiguous lesson references. It cannot determine whether explanatory prose is still true; that remains a review responsibility.

The interactive labs are deliberately limited teaching models, not alternative SDK implementations. They simulate only the rules they name, assume valid supporting conditions unless a control says otherwise, and do not test the real backend. Use the Kotlin tests and independent consumers for implementation evidence.

Use the source explorer for exact implementation detail. Use the change recipes for the smallest sensible edit scope. Keep this document local unless you intentionally decide to share the repository source embedded in it.

quiz.question: After you rename a field and all Kotlin code compiles, what might still need attention?
options: Persisted serialization, external public callers, provider mapping, behavior tests and guide examples affected by the field
Every SDK module must get a new interface
quiz.explanation: Compilation checks one set of callers. Stored data and external consumers can still rely on the old representation or contract; focus on the actual affected boundaries.
